analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal contracts with private, for-profit prison and halfway-house companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Justice Department to phase out its contracts with private companies that run federal prisons and halfway houses, and would have written into law that the core work of housing, guarding, and disciplining federal prisoners must be done by government employees rather than for-profit contractors. It also added oversight measures, including annual inspections of jails holding federal detainees, and required prisons to give people leaving custody help with expungement, jobs, public benefits, and voting registration.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in privately run federal prisons and halfway houses, who would be housed and supervised by government employees under mandatory public standards instead of companies paid per inmate. Federal corrections workers would gain the work currently contracted out. People leaving federal prison would gain required help with record expungement, jobs, Medicaid, food assistance, and voting registration.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that, starting six years after enactment, all core correctional services at every facility used by the Bureau of Prisons or U.S. Marshals Service be performed by federal employees, with a narrow exception for state and local government-run jails [S3].

Bans the Bureau of Prisons from contracting with for-profit companies to run community confinement facilities starting eight years after enactment, and directs the Attorney General to phase out existing contracts in the meantime [S3].
Requires the U.S. Marshals Service to annually inspect every jail it uses to confirm it meets constitutional, federal, and state standards [S3].

Requires prerelease counseling and help with expungement, job and education programs, Medicaid, food assistance, Social Security, driver's licenses, and voter registration for people leaving federal custody [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies and halfway-house operators would lose their federal contracts and revenue. Taxpayers could face transition costs as the government hires staff or shifts inmates to public facilities, and the phase-out timeline stretched up to eight years before the ban fully took effect.

drawbacks.text: The timeline was slow: private prison contracts could continue for six years and private halfway-house contracts for eight years before the ban fully applied [S3].

Replacing contractors with federal employees could raise operating costs during the transition, and the bill included no plan for absorbing inmates currently held in private facilities beyond a general direction to phase out contracts [S3].
The bill changes who runs the facilities, not how many people are incarcerated; it does not reduce the federal prison population itself [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change—ending profit incentives in the confinement of federal prisoners and adding reentry and inspection requirements—aimed directly at a documented area of underregulated private detention, and the oversight and reentry provisions stand on their own. The cost is real but limited to a transition: government operation may cost more per bed in some cases, and the multi-year phase-out blunted the immediate effect. The larger weakness is that the bill left the size of the prison system untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then passed along to its crime subcommittee a week later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on September 26, 2017 [S1].
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction and to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations on October 4, 2017 [S5].
The complete action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the subcommittee referral [S5].

The bill's text would have barred core correctional services from being performed by private contractors after a phase-out period, and prohibited Bureau of Prisons contracts with for-profit community confinement operators [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison companies and halfway-house operators kept their federal contracts and revenue, since no move to end them advanced. The status quo in federal detention — including the administration's reversal of the prior phase-out policy — went unchallenged in Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison operators kept their contracts

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out federal private prison contracts and provided the sole sponsorship.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and allowed the bill to sit without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Department of Justice under Attorney General Jeff Sessions
against.role: Executive agency whose contracts the bill would terminate
against.what_they_did: In early 2017, rescinded the prior administration's directive to reduce and ultimately end the Bureau of Prisons' use of private prisons, reversing the phase-out this bill sought to write into law.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split — only that no Republican or Democratic member added their name [S4].

industries.industry: Private prison companies (e.g., CoreCivic, GEO Group)
industries.note: These companies are paid per inmate to house federal prisoners under Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts, so ending the contracts eliminates their federal revenue; their business model profits from the number of people confined. Because the bill died, they kept the contracts.

The bill would have barred the Bureau of Prisons from using for-profit firms to run halfway houses, removing that revenue stream while requiring federal research into which reentry programs actually work.

industries.industry: Federal corrections workforce (Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service employees)
industries.note: Core correctional work currently performed by contractors would have shifted to federal employees, moving this work into the public sector.
